FOR INDEPENDENT ATM ROUTE OPERATORS

Transaction count lies. Profit per placement doesn't.

A machine that "did 220 withdrawals this month" can still be losing you money once the location's cut, processor fees, and the cost of the cash sitting in it come out. This free calculator finds real monthly profit for one location, then rolls your whole route up into a number you can check against your income goal.

Evaluating a new placement offer before you have a machine running? See is this ATM placement worth it? for a worked example of how a withdrawal-count pitch can still lose money. Shopping for a new processor instead? See this calculator vs. ATM Depot's Profit Calculator. Already pricing placements in a spreadsheet? See this calculator vs. a spreadsheet. Trimming an existing route by transaction count? See why the busiest-looking machine can be the one losing money.

Common questions

Why does the location's cut come out of the surcharge before anything else?

Because that is how nearly every ATM placement agreement is written — the location owner is paid a percentage of the surcharge revenue, a flat monthly fee, or both, regardless of your own costs. This calculator charges that split (or flat fee) to a visit before the processor fee, vault cash cost, or your own labor.

Why is vault cash treated as a cost at all — isn't it just my own money sitting in the machine?

It is your money, which is exactly why it has a cost: cash loaded into a machine cannot earn a return anywhere else, and if a cash-servicing company loads it for you, they charge for holding it. This calculator applies an annual cost-of-capital rate to your average cash balance so that cost shows up next to the surcharge revenue it makes possible, instead of disappearing as "my own cash, no cost."

Why is the processor fee a flat amount per transaction instead of a percentage like a card fee?

Because that is how ATM processing is actually billed — a fixed fee per withdrawal to route and settle it through the network, not a percentage of the surcharge. Modeling it as a percentage would understate the cost on a machine with a low surcharge and overstate it on one with a high surcharge.

Does anything about my locations or transaction counts get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the location list you type into the route section is never saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. The visit inputs above and the target monthly income setting are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

is-this-atm-placement-worth-it.html.text:
← ATM route margin calculator

Is this ATM placement worth it?

A store owner's placement offer usually comes as an estimated withdrawal count and a proposed commission split — not a monthly profit figure. That estimate does not say whether the placement covers the location's cut, the processor fee, the cost of the cash sitting in the machine, and your own refill time. Two offers with the same "withdrawals a month" pitch can land on opposite sides of zero once those come out.

Open the free route margin calculator

What a withdrawal-count pitch hides

The commission split, before you see a dollar. Nearly every placement agreement pays the location a percentage of the surcharge, a flat monthly fee, or both — off the top, regardless of your costs. A 50% split means half of every surcharge dollar was never yours to begin with.

A flat per-transaction processor fee. Routing and settling a withdrawal costs the same fixed amount whichever way the surcharge is set, so it eats a bigger share of a low surcharge than a high one.

Vault cash cost of capital. The cash loaded into the machine either could be earning a return elsewhere or costs a cash-servicing company to hold — either way it is a real monthly cost, and it is the line most often left out of a back-of-envelope estimate because it is "your own money."

Refill labor, drive time, and the machine itself. A location across town costs more per visit than one on your existing loop, and the machine's lease or amortized cost runs whether the location is busy or slow.

Worked example

A convenience-store owner offers a placement estimated at 90 withdrawals a month, a $2.50 surcharge, a 50% commission split, no flat fee, a $0.30 processor fee, 8% annual cost of capital on a $2,000 average cash load, 4 refill visits a month at 15 minutes on-site and 20 minutes round-trip drive over 8 miles, a $0.67/mile rate, a $25/hour target rate for your own time, and a $60/month machine cost:

FigureValue
Gross surcharge revenue$225.00 (90 × $2.50)
Location commission (50%)$112.50
Processor fees$27.00 (90 × $0.30)
Vault cash cost of capital$13.33 ($2,000 at 8%/yr)
Mileage$21.44 (8 miles × $0.67 × 4 visits)
Your labor$58.33 (2.33 hrs at $25/hr)
Machine cost$60.00
Total cost$292.60
Net profit−$67.61 (−30.0% of surcharge revenue)
Profit per withdrawal−$0.75

A "90 withdrawals a month" pitch that sounds like it should clear over $100 instead loses money every month it runs — before counting anything the calculator does not model, like a slow season or a shortage on a refill. Negotiating a lower commission split or a flat placement fee instead of a percentage, or finding a location on an existing refill loop instead of a special trip, are the levers that actually move this number; raising the surcharge alone hands half of any increase straight back to the location.

Common questions

How do I know if an ATM placement offer will actually turn a profit?

Subtract the location's commission or flat fee, the per-transaction processor fee, the vault cash cost of capital, refill labor and travel, and the machine's own monthly cost from the surcharge revenue the estimated withdrawal count would bring in. A store offering 90 withdrawals a month at a $2.50 surcharge, split 50/50, looks like it should clear over $100 — after the real costs it loses about $67.61 a month instead.

Why would a placement with 90 withdrawals a month still lose money?

Because the surcharge is not the only line moving. Half of it goes to the store, the processor takes a fixed fee on every withdrawal regardless of the surcharge, the cash sitting in the machine has a cost of capital whether or not it is used, and refill visits cost drive time and mileage on top of the machine's own monthly cost. A withdrawal count that sounds busy can still leave nothing once all five come out.

Does raising the surcharge fee always fix a losing placement?

Only if the commission split does not eat the increase. A 50% commission means half of every extra dollar of surcharge goes straight to the store, so raising the fee closes the gap more slowly than it looks. A lower commission percentage or a flat placement fee instead of a percentage split often moves the number more than the surcharge fee itself.

What is vault cash cost of capital and why does it matter for a placement decision?

It is the return that cash could earn sitting somewhere else, or the fee a cash-servicing company charges to hold it — either way it is a real monthly cost of the cash loaded into the machine, not free money because it is technically still yours. Skipping it makes every placement look more profitable than it is, worst on low-volume machines where it is a larger share of a smaller surcharge.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← ATM Route Margin Calculator

ATM route margin calculator vs a spreadsheet

A route-pricing spreadsheet can total commission, processor fees, and mileage correctly if every cell is filled in. What it doesn't do on its own is charge the vault cash sitting in the machine a cost of capital -- because that cost never arrives as a bill the way a processor fee does, so nothing on a typical cost list prompts anyone to add it. On a location running a real cash balance, that omission is the difference between a route that looks healthy and one that barely clears.

What a per-location spreadsheet tracks, and what it doesn't

A per-location pricing spreadsheetThis calculator
Commission split / flat feeA cell most operators already trackCharged against gross surcharge the same way
Processor fee, mileage, laborUsually tracked once someone thinks to add the columnsItemized fields for each, held apart from the commission split
Vault cash cost of capitalNot on the sheet unless someone deliberately adds an opportunity-cost line -- it is never a bill you receiveA required field: an annual cost-of-capital rate applied to the average cash balance, every time
Route income-gap projectionA manual SUM and a manual formula someone has to writeRolls the list into total and average profit, then divides the gap to a target income by the average automatically

One location, two very different margins

Take a location doing the calculator's default 220 withdrawals a month at a $2.75 surcharge, a 40% commission split, and a $0.30 processor fee -- but running a larger cash balance, $8,000, serviced at an 18% annual cost-of-capital rate. A spreadsheet that lists commission, processor fees, mileage, and labor but never adds a line for the cash itself reports:

Gross surcharge revenue$605.00
Commission, processing, mileage, labor, machine cost$461.47
Net profit (no vault cash cost line)$143.53
Margin (no vault cash cost line)23.72%

That reads as a healthy location. Add the one line most cash-in/cash-out sheets never get around to -- $8,000 of vault cash at 18% annually costs $120.00 a month, whether that cash is your own or a servicing provider's -- and the same location comes out very differently:

Vault cash cost of capital$120.00
Net profit (vault cash cost counted)$23.53
Margin (vault cash cost counted)3.89%

Nothing about the location changed between those two readings. The $120 was always there, drawing down a return it could have earned elsewhere -- a spreadsheet just never asked. This calculator asks every time, because the cash-cost field has no default of zero worth trusting.

Why "how many more locations" needs the average held apart

Say a four-location route nets $185, $60, -$10, and $40 a month once each location's own numbers are worked out -- a spreadsheet's SUM gets the $275 total right, and AVERAGE gets $68.75 right. Neither function, on its own, answers the next question an operator actually has: against a $1,200 monthly income goal, that's a $925 gap, and closing it at the same $68.75 average takes 14 more locations. That's a formula someone has to write on purpose, and a single losing placement (-$10 here) pulls the average -- and so the projection -- down in a way that is easy to miss glancing down a column, but that this calculator's route roll-up computes on every change to the list.

Open the ATM Route Margin Calculator to price your own route, or read is this ATM placement worth it? for a worked example on a single new offer. Shopping for a new processor instead? See this calculator vs. ATM Depot's Profit Calculator.

Common questions

What does a route-pricing spreadsheet usually get right, and what does it miss?

Filled in carefully, a spreadsheet can total a location's commission split, processor fees, mileage, and labor time correctly. What it doesn't do on its own is charge the vault cash sitting in the machine a cost of capital -- because that cost never arrives as an invoice the way a processor fee or a mileage receipt does, nothing on a typical cash-in/cash-out cost list prompts anyone to add a line for it unless they already know to.

Why does vault cash need a cost line at all if it's already my own money?

Because it is money that could be earning a return somewhere else, or that a cash-servicing provider would charge to hold. An annual cost-of-capital rate applied to the average cash balance turns that opportunity cost into a monthly dollar figure next to the surcharge revenue it makes possible -- and on a location running a large cash balance, that figure can be the difference between a route that looks healthy and one that is barely breaking even.

Why can't a running list of per-location profit numbers tell me how many more locations I need?

A spreadsheet can sum a column of monthly profit figures and average them without much trouble. What it usually doesn't do automatically is divide the gap between that total and a monthly income goal by the average profit per location, to say how many more placements at the same average would close it -- and a route carrying even one underperforming or losing location pulls that average down in a way that is easy to miss just eyeballing a list, but that changes the answer directly.

Does this calculator store or upload anything I type?

No. Every field runs in your browser and nothing survives closing the tab except the visit-cost inputs and income goal, which are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off from the calculator page.

vs-atm-depot.html.text:
← ATM Route Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. ATM Depot's Profit Calculator

One tool pitches switching a single machine to a new processor. This one prices every location on the route you already run, from the placement agreement you actually have. They answer different questions for different moments in the business.

What each one is for

ATM Depot's Profit Calculator is a free lead tool published by ATM Depot, an ATM equipment and processing vendor. It compares what a single machine currently earns to what ATM Depot's own processing and rebate would pay instead, to show how much switching could increase your take — and getting the personalized quote or the accompanying PDF guide asks for your name and email. It is aimed at someone deciding whether to move a machine's processing to ATM Depot, not at pricing a whole route of independently-placed machines from their real agreements.

This calculator does the other job: it prices every location on your route from the placement agreement you already have. It takes the location's commission split or flat placement fee, the per-transaction processor fee you already pay, an annual cost-of-capital rate on the vault cash sitting in the machine, and your own refill and drive time, and turns that into real monthly profit per location — then rolls the whole list up and checks it against a monthly income goal. A single-machine switching estimate has no field for any of that, because it is not built to answer that question.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Would a new processor pay more on this one machine?ATM Depot's Profit Calculator — a single-machine switching estimate from an equipment and processing vendor.
Which of my current placements are actually worth keeping?This calculator — free, private, no account, no email.
How much does the location's commission split or flat fee actually take off the top?This calculator. A processor-switching estimate has no field for a placement agreement's terms.
Does my route clear a monthly income goal once refill travel and vault cash cost are counted?This calculator's route roll-up — not something a single-machine estimate checks.
Do I need to give up my email address to see a number?This calculator: no. ATM Depot's tool asks for your name and email to send a quote.
Price your own route

This calculator needs no account, no email, and no upload: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved when you close the tab.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ATM Depot's Profit Calculator?

They do different jobs. ATM Depot is an ATM equipment and processing vendor, and its free Profit Calculator compares what a single machine currently earns to what ATM Depot's own processing and rebate would pay instead — a lead tool built to win your processing business, aimed at one machine. This calculator instead prices every location on your own route from the placement agreement you actually have: the location's commission split or flat fee, the processor fee you already pay, the cost of the vault cash sitting in the machine, and your own refill and travel time, then rolls the whole list up and checks it against a monthly income goal. If you are shopping for a new processor, their tool tells you what switching could pay. If you already know your costs and want to know which of your locations are actually worth keeping, this one does.

Does this calculator ask for my email or contact information?

No. Getting a personalized quote or the free PDF guide from ATM Depot's site asks for your name and a valid email address, because it is built to start a sales conversation. This calculator needs neither an email nor an account — it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved when you close the tab.

Does ATM Depot's calculator account for the location's commission split, vault cash cost, or refill travel time?

Not as far as its own published page describes: it is framed around one machine's surcharge revenue and processing rebate, to show how much switching to ATM Depot could increase your take. It has no field for a location's percentage commission or flat placement fee, no cost-of-capital rate on the vault cash sitting in the machine, and no refill-visit labor, drive time, or mileage — the costs an independent route operator actually carries per stop. Those are exactly the numbers this calculator asks for, because they are what decide whether one placement is worth keeping.

Is this page affiliated with ATM Depot?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ATM Depot. ATM Depot and Profit Calculator are named here only to describe what this tool is and is not.

vs-ranking-by-transaction-count.html.text:
← ATM Route Margin Calculator

This calculator vs. ranking your route by transaction count

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic habit every route operator already has: sorting locations by monthly withdrawal count and treating the busiest machines as the best ones.

First — transaction count is not useless

A withdrawal report is real information: it tells you a location still gets foot traffic, and a machine trending toward zero withdrawals is a genuine problem worth acting on. Nothing below argues for ignoring that report. What it argues is that count alone cannot answer the next question — which of these locations is actually worth keeping — because count only drives one line of the arithmetic, and every other cost is set by the placement terms, not the traffic.

The worked example

Both locations below process the identical 220 withdrawals this month at the same $2.75 surcharge fee — so a transaction-count ranking would place them side by side. The only things that differ are the commission split, the size of the vault cash load, and the drive to service the machine.

FigureLocation A — 25% commission, $2,000 cash, 10-min driveLocation B — 55% commission, $5,000 cash, 35-min drive
Monthly withdrawals220220 — identical
Gross surcharge revenue$605.00$605.00 — identical
Location commission$151.25 (25%)$332.75 (55%)
Processor fees$66.00$66.00 — identical
Vault cash cost of capital$13.33 ($2,000 at 8%/yr)$33.33 ($5,000 at 8%/yr)
Mileage cost$10.72$58.96
Your refill labor$41.67 (1.67 hrs)$83.33 (3.33 hrs)
Net monthly profit$262.03 (43.3% margin)−$29.38 (−4.9% margin)
Profit per withdrawal$1.19−$0.13
Price your own route Evaluating a new offer instead? →

Every figure above is this calculator's own arithmetic on the two location profiles described, not a claim about any real route or an industry benchmark. Your commission splits, cash loads, and drive times will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to check, not what they should come out to.

The two places a transaction-count ranking goes quiet

1. It cannot see the placement terms behind the count

A withdrawal report has one column. It cannot show that Location B's 55% commission takes more than double the cut Location A's 25% does on the identical surcharge revenue, or that the processor fee — fixed per withdrawal — already lands the same on both before commission is even subtracted. Two machines that look identical on a traffic report can be running under completely different agreements.

2. It cannot see the cash and the drive

Vault cash cost and refill mileage scale with the machine's own cash load and location, not with how many withdrawals it processes. A location that needs a larger cash float and a longer drive carries a real monthly cost a transaction count never states, which is most of the gap between Location A's $262.03 profit and Location B's $29.38 loss on the same 220 withdrawals.

When ranking by count is still the right first check

Watching withdrawal counts month to month is still the cheapest way to catch a location going quiet, and it needs no calculator. The point at which count stops being enough is when you are deciding which locations to keep, drop, or renegotiate — that decision needs the commission split, the cash load, and the drive behind each stop, which is what this calculator prices per location before rolling the whole route up against a monthly income goal.

Common questions

Is transaction count a bad way to judge a location?

Not on its own terms — it tells you the location gets foot traffic, which is real information. The problem is using it as a stand-in for profit. Two locations doing the identical 220 withdrawals a month can land on opposite sides of zero once the commission split, the vault cash sitting in the machine, and the drive to service it are counted, and a monthly report that only lists withdrawal counts has no way to show that.

How can two locations with the same withdrawal count have such different profit?

Because withdrawal count only drives one line — gross surcharge revenue — and every other cost is set by the placement terms, not the traffic. On this calculator's own worked example, both locations gross an identical $605.00 from 220 withdrawals at the same surcharge fee. One pays a 25% commission on a $2,000 cash load with a 10-minute drive; the other pays 55% on a $5,000 cash load with a 35-minute drive. The first nets $262.03. The second loses $29.38.

Which locations does this catch that a withdrawal-count ranking misses?

The ones a monthly transaction report ranks in the middle or even near the top, because it sorts by traffic, not by what the traffic is worth after the location's cut, the processor fee, and the cost of servicing the stop. A route operator dropping the lowest-count machines to trim the route can pass right over a busier machine that is actually the one losing money, and keep a quieter one that pays better per visit.

Does this replace watching my withdrawal counts?

No. Withdrawal count is still the number that tells you whether a location is getting used at all, and a machine trending toward zero withdrawals is a real problem this calculator does not need to tell you about. What it adds is the number withdrawal count cannot produce on its own: whether the traffic that is there is actually profitable once the placement's own terms are priced in.
